I would also say to the Minister that the poorest households do not have savings to fall back on, do not have the option of remortgaging, and do not have the flexibility that wealthier families have to absorb these shocks. When inflation hits 5%, 6%, or higher, it does not hit everyone equally; it is a regressive tax on those who can least afford it. I urge the Government to act now, decisively, and not wait until the crisis has already deepened before bringing forward the support that people so desperately need.

Freedom of information legislation is one of the cornerstones of open and accountable government, and any changes to it must be approached with great care. These are legitimate concerns, and they will form part of the terms of reference for the review. I also want to acknowledge the point made by several Deputies about the interaction between freedom of information law and data protection legislation, which has become an increasingly complex area since the introduction of the GDPR. Getting the balance right between the public's right to know and individuals' right to privacy is not straightforward, and I expect this to be one of the more difficult aspects of the review. I would encourage all Members with views on this matter to make written submissions to the Department once the consultation process opens. This is an opportunity to strengthen our freedom of information regime for the next generation, and I want it to be shaped by the widest possible range of voices, not just those within Government.

I have discussed this matter directly with representatives of the major platforms, and while some progress has been made, it remains far too slow and far too inconsistent across different services. Some platforms have invested heavily in automated detection tools and human moderation teams, while others continue to rely on user reporting alone, which places an unacceptable burden on victims and members of the public to identify and flag harmful content themselves. That cannot be the standard we accept going forward. The Government is committed to bringing forward the Online Safety Bill, which will place a statutory duty of care on platforms to protect users, particularly children, from harmful content, and will give the regulator real powers to impose significant fines on companies that fail to meet their obligations. I want to be clear that self-regulation has had its chance, and in too many cases it has fallen short. We have seen content remain online for hours, sometimes days, after it has been reported, causing real and lasting harm to the individuals affected and, in some tragic cases, contributing to loss of life. The Committee's work in this area has been extremely valuable in building the evidence base for legislative action, and I want to thank its members for the thoroughness of their inquiry. I would also say that international cooperation will be essential here, because these platforms operate across borders, and unilateral action by the United Kingdom alone, while important, will not be sufficient to address a genuinely global problem. We will continue to work with our international partners, including through the G7 and other forums, to ensure that the standards we are setting here are matched, as far as possible, by our allies.

dogs are slaughtered for consumption around the world every year, often after being subjected to appalling cruelty, including being beaten or boiled alive in the mistaken belief that this improves the taste of the meat. While this practice is not widespread in the United Kingdom, there is currently no specific legal prohibition on the consumption of dog meat here, and reports have emerged in recent years of dogs being stolen, and in some cases specifically bred, for this purpose. This Bill would close that gap decisively. It would send an unambiguous message that our country regards dogs, alongside cats, as companion animals deserving of the strongest legal protections, not as a food source under any circumstances. I want to be clear that this Bill is not an attack on any particular culture or community; many countries with historical associations with this practice have themselves moved to ban it, recognising the shift in public attitudes and animal welfare standards. South Korea, for instance, has taken significant legislative steps in this direction only in recent years. What this Bill does is bring our own law into line with the values that the overwhelming majority of the public in this country already hold. I have received messages of support from constituents right across the political spectrum, and from animal welfare organisations who have long called for this specific and clear prohibition, rather than relying on general animal cruelty provisions that do not adequately capture the particular harms involved here. I hope that Members on all sides of the House will support this Bill, and I look forward to working with colleagues to ensure it makes swift progress through this place.

The Sustainable Development Goals cut across almost every Department of Government, from health and education to environment and social protection, and it makes little sense for a Department whose core mandate is international development to be responsible for coordinating domestic delivery of goals that are fundamentally about how we run our own society. This is not a criticism of the officials who currently carry out that coordinating role; they do so with skill and commitment, often with limited resources. It is a criticism of the institutional architecture itself. The Committee heard evidence suggesting that a body with genuine cross-departmental authority, perhaps located within the Taoiseach's own Department, would be far better placed to drive implementation and hold individual line Ministries to account for their own goals. We have seen in other jurisdictions that where SDG implementation is anchored at the centre of government, with clear political ownership at the highest level, progress tends to be more consistent and more transparent. I would also note that civil society organisations who engage regularly with these processes have raised similar concerns to the Committee, pointing out that the current arrangement can create a sense that the goals are somehow a foreign policy or overseas development matter, rather than a domestic policy framework that applies equally to how we tackle poverty, inequality, and environmental degradation here at home. I hope the Government will give serious consideration to this recommendation, and I would welcome an update from the Secretary of State on what discussions have taken place across Departments regarding a possible change to the lead coordinating role ahead of the next reporting cycle.

We need structured, accredited training pathways that give teachers the specific skills and knowledge they need to support these children effectively, from understanding sensory processing differences to developing individualised behavioural support plans that actually work in a classroom setting. At present, far too much of this training is left to the initiative of individual teachers or schools, rather than being embedded systematically within initial teacher education and ongoing professional development. I have spoken to a number of teachers in ASD-specific settings in my own constituency, and while their dedication is genuinely inspiring, many of them told me candidly that they felt they were learning on the job, often through trial and error, because the formal training available to them before they took up their posts was simply inadequate to the demands of the role. This is not fair to the teachers, and it is certainly not fair to the children in their care, who deserve to be taught by professionals with the full range of skills and confidence that the role requires. I would ask the Minister to consider establishing a dedicated national training framework, developed in consultation with special education experts, parents, and teachers themselves, that would set out clear competencies and provide accredited pathways for teachers moving into this area of work. We should also look at whether financial incentives or additional allowances might help attract more teachers into this specialism, given the additional demands the role places on them. Investing properly in this training is not an optional extra; it is fundamental to ensuring that every child, regardless of their needs, receives the education they are entitled to.

Clear, consistent, and where possible, Russian-language communication about the purpose and targets of these measures will be essential if we are to maintain both international unity and, over time, the possibility of building bridges with a future Russia that has moved beyond this era of aggression.

I know that mental health provision within professional sport, and indeed within football specifically, has too often lagged behind the scale of the challenge that players, staff, and indeed supporters face. It is welcome that the FA has chosen to use its platform to highlight this issue, but as the hon. Member has rightly pointed out, campaigns and awareness weekends, however well-intentioned, cannot substitute for genuine structural change within the sport itself. The Government has been clear in its engagement with football's governing bodies that financial arrangements within the game must reflect a broader sense of responsibility, not just to shareholders and to the wealthiest clubs, but to the wider footballing family, including lower league clubs, grassroots facilities, and the welfare of players at every level. I would say to the hon. Member that we continue to press football authorities on precisely this point, and the Government stands ready to legislate should voluntary reform prove insufficient, as we have already signalled through our response to the fan-led review. On the specific issue of mental health support, I can confirm that the Government is working closely with sporting bodies to ensure that appropriate resources and referral pathways are available not just to elite players, who often have access to significant medical support, but to those further down the football pyramid, where such provision is frequently far more limited. I would also note that former players' associations have done valuable work in this space, supporting individuals long after their playing careers have ended, when the transition out of professional sport can itself be a significant trigger for mental health difficulties. I hope the hon. Member will continue to raise these issues, because sustained parliamentary pressure has, in my experience, been an important part of driving genuine change in this area.

I would also like to understand what lessons have been incorporated into subsequent procurement processes as a result of this case. Have the contract terms for future public works been tightened to place more of the risk of unforeseen conditions on the contractor rather than the taxpayer? Madeleine trained during a time when the nursing profession demanded extraordinary resilience, long hours on her feet, limited resources, and an almost constant confrontation with human suffering, and yet she carried herself throughout her career with a warmth and a gentleness that her colleagues and patients remember to this day. Those who knew her describe a woman of remarkable generosity, who gave not out of obligation but out of a genuine and abiding love for the people around her. She never sought recognition for her efforts, believing simply that helping others was its own reward, but today, in this House, I want to make sure that recognition is given nonetheless. Madeleine's legacy lives on not only in the countless patients whose lives she touched, but in the values she instilled in her family and in the many young nurses she mentored over the years, who continue to carry forward her spirit of compassion in their own careers. On behalf of this House, I extend my deepest condolences to Madeleine's family, and I thank them for sharing her remarkable spirit with all of us. May her memory be a blessing, and may her example continue to inspire generations of caregivers to come.

That means keeping open channels of communication, even at moments of heightened tension, because history has repeatedly shown us that miscalculation, rather than deliberate escalation, is often the greater risk when diplomatic contact breaks down entirely. I would also say to the House that sanctions and diplomacy are not mutually exclusive; indeed, they are most effective when pursued in tandem. Sanctions serve to signal seriousness of intent and to impose real costs on behaviour we cannot accept, while diplomacy provides the pathway through which those costs can eventually be lifted in exchange for verifiable changes in conduct. We saw this dynamic play out, imperfectly but not without some success, in the negotiations that led to the original nuclear agreement, and I believe the lessons of that process remain relevant today, even as circumstances have changed considerably in the intervening years. I would urge the Government to continue working closely with our European partners and with regional allies who have a direct stake in the outcome of these discussions, because a durable solution cannot be imposed from outside; it must be negotiated with full regard to the legitimate security concerns of all parties involved, difficult as that balance undoubtedly is to strike. I recognise that trust between the parties involved is at a low ebb, and rebuilding it will not happen overnight. But the alternative, a region drawn ever closer to open conflict, with all the humanitarian and strategic consequences that would entail, is simply not one that this House, or indeed the international community more broadly, should be willing to accept without having exhausted every diplomatic avenue available to us first.

I think of the Argentine conscripts, many barely out of their teens, sent into a war they had little say in starting, poorly equipped and poorly prepared for the harsh conditions of the South Atlantic winter. Their families, too, carry the weight of that loss, just as surely as the families of the British and Falklands casualties do. Reconciliation between our two nations has been a long and, at times, difficult process, but it has been a necessary one, and I believe it reflects well on both countries that we have been able to build a relationship based on mutual respect, even while fundamental disagreements about sovereignty remain unresolved. On this anniversary, I think it is right that we honour the service and sacrifice of our own personnel and the Falkland Islanders who lost their lives, while also recognising the shared humanity of loss on the other side of that conflict. This is precisely the kind of selective concern that undermines the credibility of some of the arguments made against pipeline transport more broadly. If our genuine priority is minimising environmental risk, we need to look honestly at the comparative safety record of all available transport methods, rather than focusing exclusively on the option that happens to be the most visible or the most politically convenient target of the moment. I am not suggesting that pipeline transport carries zero risk; no method of transporting hazardous materials is without risk, and this Government takes seriously its responsibility to ensure the highest possible safety standards are applied, regardless of the transport method chosen. But if we are going to have an honest debate about how best to move these products safely, we cannot simply default to opposing pipelines while ignoring the fact that the alternative, increased rail transport, carries its own well-documented risks to both waterways and communities along those rail corridors. I would encourage members opposite to engage with the full body of evidence on this question, rather than relying on the assumption that opposition to pipelines is automatically the more environmentally responsible position, when the data suggests a considerably more complicated picture.

The health centre has served this rural community faithfully for many decades, providing not just general practice services but a range of primary care supports that would otherwise require patients, many of them elderly and without reliable transport, to travel considerable distances to access. I raise this matter today because there is growing concern locally about the future of the centre, following reports that funding for necessary upgrades and staffing has not been forthcoming at the level required to maintain the current standard of service. This is a part of the country that already faces significant challenges in terms of access to healthcare, given its rural and, in places, quite remote geography, straddling as it does the border between two counties. The loss, or even the diminishment, of services at Fourmilewater would have a disproportionate impact on some of the most isolated communities in the region, many of whom have no realistic alternative within a reasonable distance. I have spoken with local residents, with the GP currently attached to the centre, and with community representatives, and the message I have received consistently is one of deep concern about the sustainability of current arrangements. I would ask the Minister to provide clarity on what plans, if any, exist for the future of this centre, and specifically whether the necessary capital and staffing investment will be forthcoming to ensure it can continue to serve this community for years to come. Rural healthcare provision cannot simply be left to wither through neglect while resources are concentrated in larger urban centres; the people of these parishes pay their taxes and are entitled to the same standard of access to primary care as anyone living closer to a major hospital or urban GP practice.

Size alone is not, and should not be treated as, a reliable proxy for risk. We have seen, time and again, that some of the most harmful content and activity online can originate from or spread through smaller, more niche platforms, precisely because those platforms often attract communities that have been pushed out of, or deliberately avoid, the larger mainstream platforms where content moderation, however imperfect, is at least more robustly resourced. I understand the Government's concern about proportionality, and I do not think anyone in this House wants to see small, genuinely low-risk platforms, such as hobbyist forums or small community websites, burdened with compliance requirements designed for organisations with the resources of the largest technology companies in the world. But the solution to that legitimate concern is not to exempt platforms based on size alone; it is to build genuine risk-based tiering into the regulatory framework, so that the intensity of regulatory obligation scales with the actual risk profile of the platform, rather than a crude proxy like user numbers or revenue. I hope the Minister will engage constructively with the amendment I intend to table on this point, because getting this balance right is essential if this legislation is to achieve its stated purpose of genuinely protecting users from online harm.

That is precisely why the Government has committed to a clear public information campaign, so that the overwhelming majority of policyholders, who fall comfortably within the exempted threshold, understand clearly that this change simply does not affect them, and that this measure is targeted specifically and narrowly at addressing an area of genuine unfairness in how our tax system currently operates.

Multiculturalism as a federal policy exists precisely because we recognise that Canada's strength comes from the diversity of the communities that make up our national fabric, and that recognition should not, and cannot, be selectively applied depending on which province a person happens to call home. Quebec's ethnocultural and religious communities are just as much a part of that national fabric as communities anywhere else in this country, and carving out an exemption of this kind sends the deeply troubling message that their experiences, their needs, and their contributions somehow fall outside the scope of a policy explicitly designed to support communities exactly like theirs. I understand that this proposal is rooted in genuine and long-standing debates within Quebec about the particular model of interculturalism that the province has developed, distinct in important ways from the federal multiculturalism framework. I do not dismiss those debates as illegitimate; Quebec has every right to pursue its own approach to integration and cultural accommodation within its own areas of jurisdiction. But federal programs exist to serve federal purposes, and carving out a formal legislative exemption undermines the coherence of a national framework that has, for decades, helped newcomers and minority communities across this entire country access support, recognition, and a genuine sense of belonging within the Canadian project. I would urge members to consider carefully what precedent this sets, not just for Quebec, but for the principle of national programs more broadly, and whether we genuinely want to move toward a model where federal support for minority communities becomes something to be negotiated away, province by province, rather than guaranteed equally to all Canadians regardless of where they live.

The Sewel convention exists precisely to provide a mechanism through which the boundaries between reserved and devolved competence are respected in practice, not simply in the abstract language of the devolution statutes themselves. When this convention is set aside, as it has been on a number of occasions in recent years in relation to legislation with clear implications for devolved matters, it sends a troubling signal about how seriously this Government regards the constitutional settlement it inherited and, indeed, helped to shape. I want to be clear that this is not a question of whether Scotland should have a veto over UK-wide legislation; nobody on these benches has argued for that, and it would be a mischaracterisation to suggest otherwise. What we are arguing for is simply that where legislation touches on matters that were explicitly and deliberately devolved to the Scottish Parliament, the convention requiring consent should be respected as a matter of course, save in genuinely exceptional circumstances, rather than treated as an optional courtesy that can be bypassed whenever it proves politically inconvenient for the Government of the day. I would ask the Minister to explain what criteria are being applied when the Government decides that legislative consent, though sought, need not actually be secured before proceeding. If those criteria are not clear and consistently applied, we risk a steady erosion of the devolution settlement through a thousand small exceptions, each perhaps individually justifiable, but cumulatively corrosive to the trust that underpins the entire arrangement.

Vulture funds, in particular, have been allowed to purchase distressed mortgage books at a steep discount, only to pursue full recovery from homeowners who had no say whatsoever in the sale of their loan, and who often find themselves dealing with entities that have little interest in sustainable, long-term solutions and every interest in maximising short-term recovery, including through repossession where that proves more profitable. I would ask the Taoiseach to commit to a genuine review of the protections currently available to distressed borrowers, including consideration of a statutory right to a mortgage-to-rent arrangement on terms that families can actually sustain, and stronger regulatory oversight of how unregulated loan owners and their servicing agents conduct themselves when dealing with families in genuine financial distress. The current framework has failed too many people for far too long, and incremental tweaks are simply not sufficient to the scale of the crisis we continue to face.

Irish peacekeepers have earned a reputation, internationally, for professionalism, for impartiality, and for a particular sensitivity to the needs of local populations that has, on many occasions, been specifically praised by the communities we have served in, from Lebanon to the Golan Heights to countless missions across Africa. This reputation was not built overnight, and it was not built without cost; we have lost brave members of our Defence Forces in the course of peacekeeping service, and their sacrifice deserves to be remembered and honoured as we continue to debate our future role on the world stage. I would say to those Members who have expressed alternative views on our engagement at the United Nations that our tradition of military neutrality, combined with active engagement in peacekeeping and multilateral diplomacy, is not a passive or an isolationist position; it is, in fact, an active and deliberate choice that has given Ireland a unique and valued voice in international affairs, precisely because we are not seen as aligned with any particular military bloc or great power. That neutrality has allowed us to act as honest brokers in conflicts where nations with more overt military alliances might struggle to gain the trust of all parties involved. I believe this tradition remains as relevant and as valuable today as it has ever been, and I would urge this House to continue supporting the kind of engaged, principled multilateralism that has defined our contribution to the United Nations for over six decades.

Since our Bill was voted down, we have continued to hear from communities right across this country who are still waiting for meaningful action on this issue, an issue that this Government has had ample opportunity to address through its own legislative proposals, yet has failed to do so with anything approaching the urgency the situation demands. We heard about the loss of language, of culture, of identity that was stolen from generation after generation of Indigenous children, forcibly removed from their families and communities and placed into institutions whose explicit purpose, in the words of those who designed this system, was to kill the Indian in the child. What troubles me about the debate we have heard today is a persistent tendency, whether deliberate or unconscious, to speak of these events as though they belong safely to a distant and closed chapter of our history, rather than as a system whose consequences continue to reverberate through Indigenous communities across this country in the present day, in the ongoing crisis of missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls, in the vastly disproportionate rates of incarceration and child apprehension affecting Indigenous families, and in the persistent gaps in health, education, and basic infrastructure that Indigenous communities continue to endure, gaps that exist not by accident, but as the direct and continuing legacy of policies this Parliament itself enacted and sustained for well over a century. Reconciliation cannot simply mean issuing apologies, however sincerely meant, for events safely confined to the past, while continuing to underfund the very communities still living with the consequences of those events today. I would ask members of this government to reflect honestly on how many of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's ninety-four calls to action have actually been fully implemented, rather than simply announced with considerable fanfare and then left to languish, underfunded and incomplete, in the years that follow. Survivors did not share their most painful and personal experiences with this country simply so that we could feel appropriately moved for an afternoon of debate; they did so with the expectation that meaningful, structural change would follow. That expectation has not yet been met.
